- China holds a dominant position in securing critical minerals across Africa, outpacing Western competitors.
- Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo detained about 300 Chinese nationals during a crackdown on illegal mining in the copper-rich region of Kolwezi.
- The crackdown highlights the legal and regulatory complexities China faces as it expands its mineral interests in central Africa.
- Massive Chinese investment has significantly increased Congo’s copper production, but unauthorized mining on private concessions remains a major issue.
The enforcement action reveal the complex legal and regulatory challenges accompanying China's multi-billion-dollar mineral expansion in central Africa.
DR Congo detains 300 Chinese nationals in copper hub crackdown
Security forces from Congo's National Security Council and immigration authorities carried out a targeted operation in the mining hub of Kolwezi, taking around 300 Chinese workers into custody.
According to a report by miningmx, officials conducted the arrests over "their alleged involvement in illegal mining on concessions belonging to other companies".
While massive Chinese investments have allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to triple its copper output since 2015 (becoming the world's second-largest copper producer) unauthorized mining on private corporate concessions remains a persistent challenge.
Following formal diplomatic intervention by the Chinese embassy in Kinshasa, local authorities released several of the detained workers.
China beats the US in securing Africa's critical minerals supply chain
Beijing's long-term industrial planning has given state-backed companies a decisive lead over Western rivals in controlling raw materials needed for electric vehicles, defense systems, and clean energy technology.
China currently commands over half of global critical minerals production and roughly 87% of global processing and refining capacity.
In a report published by the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, expert Paul Nantulya notes that "China has gained a dominant position in Africa's critical minerals sector through long-term investments in mining and refining capacity".
Within 20 years, Beijing channeled approximately $24 billion in transition mineral loans and credit to African nations, acquiring major mining assets in countries like Botswana, Mali, Tanzania, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

articles.title: Al-Wazir urges faster work on 500-km Sinai railway, planned 1,000-factory zone - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Al-Wazir urges faster work on 500-km Sinai railway, planned 1,000-factory zone - Urban & Transport - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Transport Minister Kamel Al-Wazir called for faster construction of Egypt’s approximately 500-kilometre Sinai railway and a planned industrial logistics zone near Arish Port, housing 1,000 factories, the ministry stated on Sunday.
The railway, extending from Ferdan through East Port Said, Bir Al-Abd and Arish to Taba, forms part of the Arish–Taba logistics corridor, designed to connect production centres with seaports and integrate Sinai into the national transport network.
During a meeting with North Sinai MPs and senior transport officials, Al-Wazir reviewed construction of the 83-kilometre Bir Al-Abd–Arish section, including earthworks and seven stations serving villages, residential communities and key facilities along the route.
The review also covered a 12-kilometre rail connection to Arish Port, a separate connection to a cement factory, and engineering works including crossing bridges, a railway bridge and tunnels.
The meeting follows Saturday reports that railway tracks reached Arish for the first time since 1967.
Al-Wazir instructed contractors to accelerate work on embankments and stations while meeting technical specifications, quality standards and agreed schedules, in line with President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi’s directives to advance development in Sinai.
He also invited Egyptian companies and specialist construction contractors from Sinai to participate, saying their involvement would create jobs for residents and help local communities benefit directly from development spending.
The minister stressed the need to expedite the planned industrial logistics zone in the hinterland of Arish Port. He said the zone, ordered by El-Sisi, is intended to accommodate 1,000 factories and expand North Sinai’s industrial base.
The railway connection accompanies the Arish Port expansion, which includes four cement silos with a combined capacity of 40,000 tonnes.
Al-Wazir said the railway is a key component of the Arish–Taba corridor, one of eight integrated international logistics corridors the transport ministry is developing.
The corridor aims to link residential, industrial and mining communities with the national railway network, facilitate passenger and freight transport, and strengthen connections between the Mediterranean and Red Sea.
He added that the project would support investment in industry, mining, agriculture and tourism, reduce freight costs and improve the competitiveness of Egyptian exports.
Egypt began passenger railway trials on the 100-kilometre Ferdan–Bir Al-Abd section on 7 October 2024.
The wider infrastructure programme includes five Suez Canal tunnels and seven floating bridges linking Sinai with the Canal cities, according to the cabinet’s media centre.

articles.title: Ethiopia loses East Africa's largest economy title as Tigray conflict slurs country's investment climate - Businessamlive
articles.summary: Ethiopia loses East Africa's largest economy title as Tigray conflict slurs country's investment climate  Businessamlive
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia has lost East Africa’s largest economy title for 2025, falling $24 billion behind Kenya, which has reclaimed the region’s top economic powerhouse for the first time in five years, in the International Monetary Fund (IMF)’s latest world economic outlook.
The reason advanced by global economic analysts is, mainly due to the depreciation of the Ethiopian birr, which reduced the dollar value of its economy amid renewed security challenges in the Tigray region, as Kenya’s GDP is projected at $135.92 billion in 2025, ahead of Ethiopia’s $126.35 billion, with the gap expected to widen to $24 billion in 2026.
Additionally, development analysts say the Tigray conflict has slurred Ethiopia’s investment climate
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has been unable to manage Ethiopia’s Tigray crisis since assuming office in 2018.
The Tigray crisis is a violent political and military struggle for power and regional control in northern Ethiopia between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which has recently reignited into a full-scale resumption of fighting
The TPLF dominated Ethiopian national politics for nearly three decades until Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018 and sidelined the party through major government reforms and the creation of the Prosperity Party. Tensions peaked in late 2020 when Tigray held unauthorized regional elections, leading to an outbreak of civil war in November 2020. Although a peace deal (the Pretoria Agreement) formally paused the 2020–2022 civil war, internal power struggles, disputed territories, and leadership rifts within the TPLF and interim administration caused the conflict to reignite in early and mid-2026.
• The multi-year conflict has caused an estimated over 800,000 deaths (including civil war casualties), mass internal displacement affecting millions, and widespread refugee flows into neighboring countries. Reports from the World Health Organisation (WHO) document widespread sexual violence, systemic infrastructure destruction, targeted blockades on food and medicine, and acute famine conditions across Tigray and neighboring Amhara and Afar regions.
Renewed insecurity in Ethiopia’s Tigray region and concerns over the 2022 peace agreement could further deter foreign investment and harm economic stability.
While Ethiopia maintains stronger real GDP growth rates than Kenya, currency movements and investor preferences have shifted economic leadership in the region back to Kenya.
According to the IMF October 2026 World Economic Outlook, Kenya’s gross domestic product (GDP) stood at $135.92 billion in 2025, surpassing Ethiopia’s $126.35 billion by $9.57 billion.
The shift marks a significant reversal in East Africa’s economic rankings, with Kenya reclaiming its position as the region’s largest economy after roughly five years.
The gap is projected to widen to $24 billion in 2026, strengthening Kenya’s standing as a regional commercial hub while Ethiopia faces currency pressures and renewed security concerns that could undermine investor confidence.
Kenya reclaims East Africa’s economic lead
Ethiopia’s economy, valued at $210 billion in 2024, fell to $126.35 billion in dollar terms in 2025 following major currency reforms.
In July 2024, the country introduced a more market-determined exchange-rate system under an IMF-supported $3.4 billion financing programme, allowing the birr to depreciate against the US dollar.
Consequently, Ethiopia’s economic output lost substantial value when converted into dollars, despite continued growth in domestic production.
Kenya, meanwhile, benefited from a relatively stable shilling, which helped preserve the dollar value of its economy.
Currency movements largely explain the reversal in rankings rather than a substantial difference in the countries’ underlying economic growth.
However, Ethiopia still has a larger economy than Kenya when measured by purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. Kenya’s lead is based on nominal GDP measured in US dollars.
Tigray conflict adds to Ethiopia’s investment challenges. While currency depreciation has reshaped the economic rankings, Ethiopia also faces renewed security challenges that could affect its investment prospects. Fresh fighting between federal forces and the Tigrayan rebels has raised concerns about the country’s stability and economic recovery.
On October 16, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a caretaker administration for Tigray after government-aligned forces regained control of the regional capital, Mekelle.
These developments have raised concerns about the durability of the 2022 peace agreement, while tensions with neighbouring Eritrea have heightened fears of wider regional instability.
The insecurity could discourage foreign investment, disrupt trade and increase operating costs, particularly for companies planning long-term infrastructure and manufacturing projects.
The IMF has also identified domestic security risks as a potential threat to Ethiopia’s economic outlook.
Meanwhile, Kenya could attract investors seeking alternative regional business locations, supported by Nairobi’s established financial services, technology and logistics sectors.
The country’s investment ambitions are reflected in Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote’s proposed $16 billion oil refinery in Lamu, a project that could strengthen Kenya’s position as an industrial and energy hub if completed.
However, Kenya continues to face economic challenges, including high public debt, borrowing costs and pressure on government finances.
Though still enmeshed in the unresolved Tigray crisis, Ethiopia however, maintains stronger economic growth despite losing top position. Despite falling behind Kenya in nominal GDP, Ethiopia continues to record stronger underlying economic growth.
IMF estimates show Ethiopia’s economy expanded by 9.2% in real terms in 2025, compared with Kenya’s 4.6%, demonstrating that the change in rankings largely reflects exchange-rate movements rather than faster growth in Kenyan production.
Looking ahead, the IMF projects Kenya’s GDP will reach $151.15 billion in 2026, compared with Ethiopia’s $127.15 billion, widening the gap between the two economies to $24 billion.
The IMF projections also place Kenya seventh among Africa’s largest economies, behind South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, Algeria, Morocco and Angola.

articles.summary: US reveals why it eased sanctions on Eritrean targets as Ethiopia, Eritrea deploy more troops and risk drawing other countries into war  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Marco Rubio says sanctions relief could improve Washington’s communication with Eritrea.
- He warned that troops gathering along the Ethiopia–Eritrea border risk a wider conflict.
- US Treasury records show the relevant sanctions removals occurred on 18 September.
- Washington has not announced a formal mediation agreement between the two countries.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington had increased contact with Eritrea in recent months and hoped sanctions relief would help preserve diplomatic access.
His explanation came as troops gathered on both sides of the border, raising concern that Ethiopia’s renewed internal fighting could develop into a confrontation involving neighbouring countries.
Speaking at Joint Base Andrews on 17 October, Rubio also said he had personally urged Ethiopian officials that week to respond with restraint.
According to the State Department’s transcript via Forth, Rubio argued that communication with both governments was necessary for any potential peacemaking role. “The last thing the world needs right now is another war,” he said.
Which sanctions ended?
The financial restrictions were removed a month before Rubio’s remarks.
The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control announced on 18 September that the national emergency underpinning its Ethiopia-related sanctions programme had expired.
It consequently removed designations imposed under Executive Order 14046. The listed removals included the Eritrean Defense Forces, the ruling People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, Hidri Trust, Red Sea Trading Corporation and two Eritrean officials.
These were removals under that specific programme. The notice did not announce the cancellation of every US restriction affecting Eritrea.
Rubio’s new comments explain Washington’s diplomatic reasoning. They do not amount to a formal mediation arrangement or evidence that either government has accepted an American negotiating role.
A border confrontation beyond Tigray
The diplomatic effort comes against a worsening relationship between the two neighbours.
As BIA previously reported, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties earlier this month amid allegations of hostile activity and reports of drone attacks.
A subsequent BIA report on troop mobilisation examined the risk of renewed interstate fighting as Ethiopian forces moved towards the border. Eritrea has disputed allegations that its forces entered Ethiopia.
Fighting involving Ethiopian armed groups and a direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea are different developments, with different implications for the region.
Rubio warned that escalation could pull other countries into the confrontation. He did not name those countries or announce new US deployments, military assistance or security guarantees.
Washington’s stated approach is to maintain communication with both governments while pressing for restraint. Whether that access produces negotiations remains unresolved.

articles.title: Ethiopia Takes Made in Ethiopia Into Export Phase - Uchumi360
articles.summary: Ethiopia Takes Made in Ethiopia Into Export Phase  Uchumi360
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia Revives 1,115 Factories, Creates 1.58 Million Jobs as Made in Ethiopia Shifts to Exports
Ready
Ethiopia says its Made in Ethiopia initiative revived 1,115 factories, created 1.58 million jobs and generated US$5.96 billion in import substitution between 2021 and 2025. The next phase will focus on exports, new capacity and industrial services, shifting the programme from domestic factory recovery towards the harder test of international competitiveness.
Ethiopia is preparing to take its “Made in Ethiopia” industrial programme into a more difficult phase after the government said the initiative revived 1,115 factories, created 1.58 million jobs and generated US$5.96 billion worth of import substitution between 2021 and 2025. The Ministry of Industry says the next stage will concentrate on expanding manufactured exports, adding new productive capacity and modernising the services that support industry, marking an important shift in the programme’s economic purpose. The first phase was largely about getting more out of an industrial base Ethiopia already possessed: reopening factories that had stopped operating, raising utilisation at plants working below capacity, reducing dependence on imported finished goods and creating employment around domestic production. The next phase asks a more demanding question. It is one thing for Ethiopian factories to replace goods that would otherwise have been imported into a domestic market affected by foreign exchange shortages, transport costs and government policies favouring local production. It is considerably harder for the same factories to persuade buyers outside Ethiopia to choose their products over alternatives manufactured in China, India, Turkey, Egypt, Kenya, Vietnam and other competing production centres. If Ethiopia succeeds, “Made in Ethiopia” could evolve from an import substitution programme into something much closer to an export industrialisation strategy.
The scale of the official results explains why the programme is being extended.
Reviving 1,115 factories means Ethiopia has attempted to recover productive assets that already contained capital in the form of machinery, factory buildings, established workforces and industrial knowledge rather than relying entirely on building new plants.
The reported creation of 1.
58 million jobs suggests that the government views industrial expansion not only through the value of manufacturing output but also through its ability to absorb a rapidly growing labour force, while the US$5.
96 billion attributed to import substitution points towards another equally important objective: reducing Ethiopia’s persistent demand for foreign exchange.
For an economy that has experienced years of hard currency shortages, replacing imported finished products with locally manufactured alternatives can produce benefits even before those factories become internationally competitive, because each product manufactured domestically potentially reduces part of the dollar demand that would otherwise be required to purchase the equivalent product abroad.
The economic value of that substitution, however, depends heavily on how much of the production chain has actually moved inside Ethiopia.
A factory that assembles imported components can replace a finished import while still requiring substantial foreign currency for machinery, spare parts and intermediate inputs, whereas industries built around Ethiopian agricultural products, minerals, labour and energy can retain a much larger share of value domestically.
The US$5.
96 billion figure is therefore significant, but the deeper measure of industrial progress will increasingly be how much domestic value Ethiopia adds to each product rather than simply the gross value of goods no longer imported.

Ethiopia First Had to Make Its Existing Factories Work
The design of the first phase addressed a problem common across developing economies where governments spend heavily attracting industrial investment while a significant share of installed manufacturing capacity remains idle or underused. A factory operating at 40 or 50 percent of capacity has already absorbed much of the expensive capital required to establish production, including land, buildings, machinery and basic infrastructure, yet still produces far below what those assets were designed to deliver. Increasing utilisation at such a plant can therefore raise industrial output much faster and at a lower incremental capital cost than constructing an entirely new factory. Ethiopia’s decision to focus on dormant and underperforming plants recognised that industrialisation is not only about announcing new investment projects but also about identifying why existing firms are unable to produce. In Ethiopia’s case, those constraints have included shortages of foreign exchange for industrial inputs, limited access to finance, interruptions in raw material supply, infrastructure problems, logistics costs and the difficulty some local producers have faced competing with imported goods. Bringing more than a thousand factories back into production, if sustained, matters because it represents the recovery of capital that had effectively been removed from the productive economy.
This approach also helps explain why the programme could produce large employment gains relatively quickly. Industrial job creation does not depend only on the workers standing inside a factory. Manufacturing creates demand for transport, packaging, maintenance, warehousing, agricultural inputs, professional services, wholesale distribution and other activities surrounding production, meaning that the economic employment impact can extend beyond direct factory payrolls. The reported 1.58 million jobs should nevertheless be interpreted carefully unless the government publishes a detailed breakdown separating permanent direct manufacturing employment from temporary, indirect and value chain jobs, because these categories have very different implications for productivity and household income. A manufacturing job in a productive factory that continuously sells goods can generate wages and skills for years, while employment associated with plant construction or temporary investment activity has a different economic character. As Ethiopia moves into the next phase, employment reporting would become more informative if it showed not only how many jobs were created but also which industries created them, how many are permanent, what workers earn and how output per employee is changing. An industrial programme ultimately succeeds not simply by employing more people, but by moving workers into increasingly productive activities that support higher incomes.
The significance of factory revival should also be understood against Ethiopia’s broader ambition to alter the structure of its economy. The country has spent years pursuing manufacturing through industrial parks, infrastructure investments, textile and apparel production, agro processing, leather, pharmaceuticals and other sectors, yet manufacturing remains much smaller as a share of the economy than would be expected in a deeply industrialised country. Restoring idle plants can produce a strong initial improvement without necessarily changing that structure quickly. Ethiopia therefore needs to distinguish between recovering from previously low capacity utilisation and creating a sustained industrial acceleration in which manufacturing grows faster than the rest of the economy over many years. The first is a recovery story. The second is structural transformation. “Made in Ethiopia” will ultimately be judged by whether the factory revival becomes the beginning of the latter.
The US$5.96 Billion Import Substitution Figure Shows Both the Achievement and the Limitation
Import substitution has provided Ethiopia with an obvious starting point because the country possesses a large domestic market and has faced severe foreign exchange constraints. Every time a locally produced product replaces an imported finished good, Ethiopia potentially preserves foreign currency that can instead be used to purchase machinery, fuel, medicines, industrial components and other imports that are more difficult to replace domestically. This logic is particularly attractive in an economy where access to dollars has frequently constrained businesses themselves, because manufacturers often struggle to import the inputs required to operate while the economy simultaneously spends foreign currency importing consumer products that could theoretically be produced locally. The US$5.96 billion attributed to import substitution therefore represents more than an industrial output statistic. If the underlying production has meaningful domestic content, it represents a reduction in one of the structural pressures that has repeatedly affected Ethiopia’s balance of payments.
The challenge is that import substitution can only carry an industrial strategy so far. Ethiopia cannot indefinitely increase manufacturing simply by taking market share away from imports because eventually the easiest products to manufacture locally will already have been substituted and industrial expansion will depend increasingly on growth in domestic consumption or access to foreign markets. In some industries, there is also a danger that domestic protection can hide weaknesses that only become visible when companies are exposed to international competition. A manufacturer serving the Ethiopian market may be able to operate with higher production costs, inconsistent quality or slow delivery if imported competitors face currency shortages, tariffs, transport costs or regulatory restrictions. The same company has no such protection when attempting to sell into another country. International buyers compare suppliers across multiple markets and can shift orders quickly when another manufacturer offers a better combination of price, quality, reliability and delivery time.

articles.title: Ghana set to overtake Ethiopia as Africa’s eighth-largest economy, leading by $1.49 billion in latest IMF projections - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Ghana set to overtake Ethiopia as Africa’s eighth-largest economy, leading by $1.49 billion in latest IMF projections  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Ghana is projected to surpass Ethiopia in Africa's economic rankings with a GDP of $128.64 billion by 2026, according to the IMF.
- Ghana's economy benefits from gold, cocoa, oil and gas exports, and a growing consumer market, with gold remaining a key export.
- Ethiopia's economy is forecast to grow faster in real terms, but depreciation of the birr has reduced its GDP in dollar terms.
- Despite Ghana's improved macroeconomic position, it faces challenges in translating this into long-term investment, jobs, and industrial growth.
The West African country is projected to rise from ninth to eighth place among Africa’s largest economies in 2026, overtaking Ethiopia, whose GDP is estimated at $127.15 billion, and staying ahead of the Democratic Republic of Congo at $122.28 billion.
Ghana’s improved ranking comes as the country continues to recover from a severe financial crisis that forced it to restructure its debt and seek IMF support.
Ghana's economic recovery strengthens its position
Ghana's economy has faced significant challenges in recent years, including currency depreciation, inflation, rising debt and pressure on government finances.
In 2023, the country secured a $3 billion IMF programme to support economic stability, restore investor confidence and address its debt problems.
Since then, Accra has pursued fiscal reforms, debt restructuring and measures aimed at stabilising prices and the cedi.
According to the IMF's latest projections, Ghana's economy is expected to expand by 5.7% in real terms in 2026, reflecting continued growth despite external economic pressures.
The country's economy also benefits from gold production, cocoa exports, oil and gas, financial services and an expanding consumer market.
Gold remains particularly important to Ghana's export earnings, while higher international prices have helped support foreign-exchange inflows.
Ghana edges ahead of Ethiopia
The latest rankings place Ghana slightly ahead of Ethiopia, although the two countries have different economic growth prospects.
Ethiopia's economy is projected to expand by 9.2% in 2026, outpacing Ghana's expected growth of 5.7%.
However, the depreciation of the Ethiopian birr following exchange-rate reforms in 2024 has reduced the country's GDP when measured in US dollars, despite strong domestic economic growth.
Ghana, meanwhile, has benefited from improving macroeconomic conditions, strengthening its position among Africa's largest economies.
Despite the shift in rankings, exchange-rate movements continue to influence nominal GDP figures, meaning Ghana's higher position does not necessarily reflect stronger underlying growth or higher living standards.
Sustaining its economic recovery will depend on Ghana's ability to attract investment, create jobs and expand industrial production.

articles.title: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta - The Sun Nigeria
articles.summary: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta  The Sun Nigeria
articles.full_text:
As Nigerians await the report of the panel set up to investigate the circumstances that led to the avoidable death of 37 artisanal miners in Niger State, it has become imperative to examine the desperation for critical minerals by non-states actors and countries like China, EU, and the US. In doing so, it is also pertinent to understand why the minerals are “critical.” A publication of the Belfer Centre for Science and International Affairs reveals the three conditions stipulated by the U.S. Energy Act of 2020 that make a mineral to be termed critical. One, the mineral has to be “essential to economic or national security.” Two, “its supply chain is vulnerable to disruption,” and three, “it performs a function in manufacturing that cannot be replaced without serious consequences, whether higher costs for key technologies, slower deployment of clean energy, or risks to defense and communications systems.”
There is another dimension that further underlines the critical element. The geopolitics of where the mineral is mined can make it critical especially, “if it is refined or processed elsewhere, particularly by a strategic rival. An example of this is China’s dominance in rare earth refining,” the Belfer Center noted. Hence, China’s likelihood of withholding supply to gain advantage is a cause for worry.
Some of these critical minerals which are inextricably connected to global transition to clean energy, production of national defense gadgetsn and artificial intelligence data storage, include copper, cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite, nickel, rare earth elements and platinum group metals (PGMs). And to follow the momentum, advanced nations continue to update their lists of critical minerals based on technological discoveries and growing appetite for them. Already, estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) as captured in Jordy Lee Calderon’s article in Milken Institute Review made a projection that the world “will require six times more mineral inputs for renewable technologies in 2040 than today,” just as the “Demand for lithium to manufacture rechargeable electricity storage, for example, is expected to increase at least 20-fold.”
In terms of global distribution, the highest reserves of critical minerals are unevenly spread across the leading nations of China, Australia, the Lithium Triangle region – (Chile, Argentina and Bolivia), Indonesia, as well as African countries like the Democratic of Congo (DRC), South Africa, Gabon, and Guinea. There are other countries in Africa including Nigeria that have significant deposits of critical minerals, but DRC alone has almost 75% of global cobalt reserves.
Meanwhile, with roughly 30% of global reserves of critical minerals, Africa is at the centre of strategic engagements for global supply, but unfortunately, the continent lacks the technical and technological capabilities to refine the minerals locally.
What is therefore witnessed in the continent is mostly raw extraction for exports by artisanal miners, factions and fractions of criminal cartels of the elites, as well as some powerful officials in government who exploit the weak regulatory environment to rip off their countries.
As such, the continent has inadvertently turned into battlegrounds for all manner of indigenous and external interests, with the mining sector morphing into a new rent-seeking frontier in Africa.
The 80% control of critical minerals processing and refining by China has also awoken the U.
S.
from passivity.
The irony, according to Calderon, is that it was the U.
S.
that “invented the complex industrial processes used for separating rare earth elements decades ago, then ceded production to China.
” For years, the U.
S.
and some other industrialized nations looked down on mining and metals industry, and China dominated the space.
But lately, the U.
S.
is poised to square up to China by extending its tentacles to African critical minerals sector.
The U.
S.
and E.
U.
have brokered deals to secure supplies from Africa.
And with Chinese companies already operating in some regions in Africa, including Nigeria, the battle may not be in the interest of the continent if they fail to act together.

The major challenge is that the mining sector in Africa is not strongly regulated amid the “new scramble”. Nigeria is still playing politics by pampering the big illegal miners who became billionaires overnight without verifiable economic production. Beyond that, Abraham Nunbogu and Kaveh Madani of Institute for Water, Environment and Health, United Nations University have raised concerns about creating “sacrifice zones” with the enormous amounts of water needed for minerals extraction and the health hazards in host communities in Africa and South America. They noted that, “In 2024 alone, global lithium production required an estimated 456 billion litres of water. That is equivalent to the annual domestic water needs of roughly 62 million people in sub‑Saharan Africa. At the same time, much of the world is facing water bankruptcy, meaning people and industries are using more fresh water than nature can replenish, leading to irrecoverable ecosystem damages.”
Besides, the communities close to the extraction sites have reportedly suffered “skin diseases, gastrointestinal illnesses, reproductive health problems and chronic health conditions associated with long‑term exposure to heavy metals in polluted water and soil…Evidence from mining regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is particularly stark. Studies document high rates of miscarriages, congenital malformations and infant mortality among populations exposed to environments contaminated with cobalt and other metals,” as noted by Nunbogu and Madani. The mining communities in Nigeria are also having their sad tales.
Indeed, Nigeria and other African nations are not doing enough to stop industrialized nations from eating their lunch. And if care is not taken, the continent will relapse into another round of “resource curse.” Efforts should be made to ensure that the resource wealth is used in a sustainable manner by negotiating as a team under a continental platform instead of doing it by individual countries. Agreements should prioritise skills development, local content, and a clear-cut plan for closure of mining sites after exploration. Nigeria should understudy how Norway made its hydrocarbon resources work for the present and future generations. Let Nigeria avoid another environmental despoilation occasioned by mining without responsibility like the Niger Delta.

articles.title: Revived 1,000 kilometers’ long, Mtwara Railway to connect the Indian Ocean with Lake Malawi in Tanzania - The Tanzania Times
articles.summary: Revived 1,000 kilometers’ long, Mtwara Railway to connect the Indian Ocean with Lake Malawi in Tanzania  The Tanzania Times
articles.full_text:
Tanzania Railways Corporation has signed a memorandum of understanding with Egypt’s Arab Contractors, covering new technical and financial work for the proposed standard gauge railway connecting Mtwara Port with Songea, Mbamba Bay.
Set to link Lake Nyasa and the Iniand Ocean, the railway line will also branch towards the Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron ore projects.
The proposed network, repeatedly described by government as approximately 1,000 kilometres, would create an east to west transport corridor across southern Tanzania, connecting the Indian Ocean with Lake Malawi while providing heavy freight infrastructure for some of the country’s largest undeveloped mineral and industrial projects.
Arab Contractors will undertake the preliminary work at its own cost and is expected to submit an initial report within three months, according to Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC) Director General Machibya Shiwa, while Transport Minister Professor Makame Mbarawa has described the agreement as “a preparatory step” and said the work must determine actual transport demand, construction costs, economic benefits and possible financing arrangements before Tanzania proceeds further.
The distinction between preparing the project and beginning construction is important because the Mtwara to Mbamba Bay railway is not a new idea and Tanzania is not studying the route for the first time.
Government has previously told Parliament that feasibility and preliminary design work had already been completed, while an earlier feasibility study dating to around 2016 was subsequently identified as requiring review before the project could be taken to investors.
By 2024, government had allocated funding for a transaction adviser to help update the project, prepare procurement documentation and examine implementation through a public private partnership, and by early 2026 officials were still describing the railway as a project whose feasibility work had been completed but whose financing remained unresolved.
The new Arab Contractors assignment should therefore be understood less as a first investigation into whether a railway can physically be built across southern Tanzania and more as an attempt to establish whether the economics of the corridor have changed sufficiently for the project to become financeable.
That question has become more relevant because several of the projects that were always supposed to provide the railway with its economic purpose are moving back onto the government’s active development agenda.
The Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron and steel projects have spent years moving between negotiation, redesign and delay, leaving the proposed railway without the large and predictable freight volumes that normally justify heavy rail infrastructure.
In 2026, however, government again signalled an intention to move the projects into implementation from 2027, while work is also progressing at Mbamba Bay Port and Mtwara continues to be positioned as a southern maritime gateway.
The railway is therefore being reconsidered at a moment when the industrial geography around it may be becoming materially different from the one that existed when the earlier feasibility study was undertaken a decade ago.
The Railway Will Ultimately Be Decided by Freight
The strongest economic case for the Mtwara to Mbamba Bay railway has never been passenger transport.
It is the movement of heavy commodities and industrial cargo over long distances at costs that road transport cannot easily match.
Mchuchuma contains approximately 428 million tonnes of identified coal reserves, while earlier development plans contemplated production of around three million tonnes of coal annually alongside a 600 MW power station.
Liganga contains roughly 126 million tonnes of identified iron ore reserves in the explored area and has historically been designed around large scale iron and steel production, with plans that have ranged from around one million tonnes of steel annually to considerably higher output under later government proposals.
If those projects begin producing at scale, the logistics problem becomes immediately obvious: millions of tons of coal, ore, steel, machinery and industrial inputs cannot be moved efficiently for hundreds of kilometres by relying predominantly on trucks without imposing high transport costs, road maintenance burdens and congestion.
This is why Mbarawa’s insistence that the new work establish real transport demand should be regarded as the central economic issue behind the agreement.
A railway of this scale carries very high fixed costs regardless of how many trains eventually run over it. Track, bridges, signalling, rolling stock, stations, maintenance facilities and associated infrastructure must all be financed before the first tonne of freight generates revenue.
The commercial question is therefore not whether southern Tanzania possesses enough resources to make the map attractive, but whether those resources can produce reliable annual cargo volumes large enough to support the capital cost of the railway.
For financiers, three million tonnes of committed coal production is much more useful than a geological reserve of hundreds of millions of tonnes that may remain underground, just as an operating steel complex provides a stronger revenue case than a proposed factory whose development timetable remains uncertain.
That relationship also works in reverse, which is one reason the corridor has been difficult to unlock.
Mining and industrial investors want confidence that their products can reach markets at competitive transport costs before committing billions of dollars to production, while railway investors want confidence that the mines and factories will exist before financing the infrastructure designed to serve them.
Tanzania therefore faces a coordination problem rather than a simple construction problem. Mchuchuma, Liganga, Mtwara Port, Mbamba Bay and the railway become substantially more valuable when developed as parts of one industrial system, but each project becomes harder to finance when the others remain uncertain.
The importance of the latest study will depend on whether it can connect those projects through credible production schedules, freight commitments and financing structures rather than simply updating engineering drawings.
Mtwara and Mbamba Bay Could Create a New Southern Trade Axis
At the eastern end of the proposed corridor sits Mtwara Port, whose long term strategic potential has always been larger than its current hinterland.
Tanzania has invested in the port partly because southern Tanzania possesses significant natural gas, agricultural and mineral resources, but maritime infrastructure can only attract large volumes when inland transport makes it economical for producers and traders to reach the coast.
Dar es Salaam has historically dominated Tanzanian international trade because it is connected to the country’s principal road and rail networks and to important inland markets in Tanzania and neighbouring states.
Mtwara has never enjoyed the same concentration of transport infrastructure, limiting the size of the commercial territory from which it can realistically draw cargo.
A railway extending through Songea and towards Mbamba Bay would materially change that calculation.
Coal, iron ore, steel, agricultural produce and manufactured goods could move towards the Indian Ocean at lower unit costs, while imported machinery, equipment, fuel and industrial inputs could travel inland.
The railway would therefore expand the effective economic hinterland of Mtwara Port rather than simply provide another transport option between existing towns. If the industrial projects along the route develop as planned, the port could increasingly function as the maritime end of a dedicated southern production corridor rather than as an infrastructure asset waiting for sufficient inland cargo to emerge.
The western end of the line has also become more economically relevant because Tanzania is investing approximately 80.56 billion, Tanzanian shillings, in the development of Mbamba Bay Port on Lake Nyasa.
During an inspection of the project in 2026, Mbarawa said the government wanted Mbamba Bay to become “a centre of trade, transport and economic activity” around the lake, with benefits extending to farmers, fishing communities and businesses.
Connecting that port to Mtwara by rail would create an east to west multimodal route linking the Indian Ocean with Lake Nyasa and potentially giving parts of Malawi and surrounding areas another path to international markets.
The regional argument, however, should not be overstated. Malawi already has access to Mozambican corridors through Nacala and Beira, while Zambia can move cargo through Dar es Salaam, Lobito, Beira and routes towards Southern African ports.
The Mtwara corridor would therefore have to win cargo commercially rather than simply exist geographically.
Freight owners will compare transport tariffs, border processing, reliability, turnaround time, storage, customs efficiency and access to shipping services.
A regional corridor becomes important when businesses choose it repeatedly because it is cheaper or more reliable than the alternatives, not because policy documents identify neighbouring countries as potential beneficiaries.
The Financing Model Matters as Much as the Engineering
The project’s financing will probably prove more difficult than its engineering.
Earlier African Union and regional infrastructure documents have attached multibillion dollar estimates to different versions of the Southern Corridor Railway, although those older numbers should not be treated as current project costs because the alignment, scope, construction prices and financing environment have changed substantially.
What remains clear is that a railway of approximately 1,000 kilometres would require an amount of capital large enough to compete with Tanzania’s other major infrastructure priorit

articles.title: Egypt’s LE2 trillion-worth infrastructure leap - Egyptian Gazette
articles.summary: Egypt’s LE2 trillion-worth infrastructure leap  Egyptian Gazette
articles.full_text:
Over the past 12 years, Egypt has expanded its infrastructure network, building new roads, bridges, transport corridors and tunnels while upgrading existing routes.
The country has also advanced major public transport projects, including the monorail and electric train, alongside the development of new cities, such as the New Capital, New Alamein and New Mansoura.
These projects aim to improve links between production facilities and urban areas, while easing pressure on established cities.
According to Ministry of Transport data, the total cost of the comprehensive plan to develop Egypt’s transport system had reached around EGP 2 trillion, of which roughly EGP530 billion was for roads and bridges.
Roads, bridges
Egypt’s National Roads Project (NRP) has seen extensive work to upgrade the road network. About 6,600 kilometres of new roads have been completed out of a planned 7,500 kilometres, alongside renovating 8,700 kilometres of the existing main road network out of a total of 10,000 kilometres.
Key new road projects include the 400-kilometre Regional Ring Road, the 156-kilometere Middle Ring Road, the 117-kilometre Galala Plateau Road, the 275-kilometre Dakhla–Sharq El Owainat Road, the 359-kilometre Toshka–Sharq El Owainat Road, the 90-kilometre Siwa–Jaghbub Road, and the 158-kilometre Beni Suef–Zafarana Road.
The state has also built and upgraded 5,000 kilometres of roads and bridges in Sinai and the Suez Canal cities since 2014 and has expanded housing and public services.
The projects include five tunnels beneath the Suez Canal, linking Sinai with the Canal cities, alongside seven floating bridges across the waterway.
Work is underway on the 660-kilometre Ain Sokhna–Alamein–Marsa Matrouh high-speed electric railway and the 500-kilometre El-Ferdan–East Port Said–Bir Al-Abd–Arish–Taba railway.
BRT
As part of the effort to upgrade the mass transit system, the first phase of the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project on the Ring Road, comprising 16 stations, has been completed, with passenger operations commencing in June 2025.
Additionally, a second phase featuring 16 stations has been executed to serve the section between the Golf Tunnel and the Cairo-Fayoum Desert Road, while planning is currently underway for a third phase, also including 16 stations.
Railway system
The Ministry of Transport has drawn up a comprehensive plan to modernise Egypt’s railway network. It is centred on six axes: rolling stock, infrastructure, signalling and control systems, maintenance workshops, staff training, and administrative and financial restructuring.
The plan aims to increase passenger capacity from around 700,000 a day in 2014 to two million by 2030. It also targets an increase in annual freight capacity from 4.5 million tonnes to 15 million tonnes over the same period.
Under the rolling stock programme, 210 new locomotives have been procured and 107 overhauled. Six luxury Talgo trains and 1,067 new passenger coaches have been delivered under a contract for 1,350 coaches. The refurbishment of 1,404 Tahya Misr passenger coaches has also been completed.
The Ministry of Transport has also received 609 freight wagons under a contract for 1,215, while 5,000 existing wagons have been rehabilitated. Procurement of seven new luxury sleeper trains and refurbishment of the existing fleet are under way.
Infrastructure upgrades have been completed at 367 of the railway network’s 709 stations. These include the new Upper Egypt railway station in Bashtil, which occupies an area four times the size of Ramses Station at the centre of Cairo.
Electronic gates, ticket-booking systems and digital payment services have also been introduced at several major railway stations, with plans to extend them to more locations.
Railway lines spanning a total of 1,634 kilometres have been renovated, alongside the modernisation of level crossings, with comprehensive upgrades completed for 822 of them.
LRT
Egypt has expanded its electric transport network in recent years, opening the first two phases of the Light Rail Transit (LRT) system. The 70-kilometre line connects Adly Mansour, 10th of Ramadan City and the New Capital.
Adly Mansour Central Station has also opened, linking six modes of transport and improving connections across the public transport network.
Metro
Cairo Metro Line 3, stretching 41.2 kilometres across four phases, is fully operational. Work continues on its fifth phase, which will extend the line to Cairo International Airport.
Cairo Metro Line 4’s first phase is scheduled to open in the first half of 2028, with construction advancing across its 19-kilometre route and 17 stations.
They include 16 underground and one surface-level station. The route begins west of the Ring Road at the 6th of October border, passing the Grand Egyptian Museum, Remaya Square, and Haram Street. It intersects with Metro Line 2 at Giza Station and Line 1 at El-Malek El-Saleh before ending at Fustat.
The government is studying three further phases for Line 4: Phase 2 from Fustat to New Cairo, Phase 3 from Hadaeq El Ashgar to Hosary Square, and Phase 4 from New Cairo to the Capital Airport.
Monorail
The East Nile Monorail was officially inaugurated by President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi last March, and commenced public passenger operations.
The East Nile Monorail project extends for 56.5 kilometres covering the distance from Cairo Stadium Station in Nasr City to the Control and Operations Centre in the New Capital.
The monorail project has created around 15,000 direct jobs in civil, electrical, and mechanical work. It has also created about 10,000 indirect jobs in related industries and services.
The East Nile Monorail integrates with Metro Line 3 at Cairo Stadium Station in Nasr City and the LRT at the Arts and Culture City Station in the New Capital.
In the future, it will integrate with the second phase of Metro Line 4 at Hesham Barakat Station in Nasr City and with Metro Line 6 at Al-Narges Station in New Cairo.
The project includes 40 trains operating at 80 km/h. Each train consists of four cars to serve urban expansion and increasing daily demand in the New Capital.
The two monorail lines (East and West Nile) extend for 100 kilometres and include 35 stations each with two levels (ticket hall and platform).
Once completed, the system will transport 500,000 passengers per day.
Meanwhile, Egypt is developing a 2,000-kilometre high-speed electric rail network with 60 stations across three lines: Sokhna–Alamein–Matrouh; October–Aswan–Abu Simbel; and Qena–Hurghada–Safaga.
New cities
Egypt has also expanded its new cities to alleviate overpopulation in the Nile Valley, modernise infrastructure, and build smart, sustainable urban centres.
The New Capital is one of the country’s major urban projects. It is designed to house key government offices and administrative, commercial and residential districts, supported by road networks, utilities and telecommunications infrastructure. Its long-term success will depend on its ability to attract residents, businesses and investment.
The New Capital is a fourth-generation city located around 60 kilometres east of Cairo and is managed by the Administrative Capital for Urban Development (ACUD).
Covering a total area of around 170,000 feddans, the city is almost four times the size of Washington D.C. and larger than some entire countries.
The New Capital hosts Egypt’s main government institutions, foreign embassies, and parliament buildings, alongside a central business district, major residential neighbourhoods, universities, and landmark cultural and religious sites, such as Misr Mosque, Al-Fattah Al-Aleem Mosque and the Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ.
It is planned to accommodate up to 10 million residents, making it one of the largest urban development projects in the region.
On the North Coast, New Alamein City is a major urban development along the Mediterranean. It stretches for around 48 kilometres along the International Coastal Road. The city is designed to operate year-round, with residential, tourism, educational, commercial and service facilities.
New Mansoura has created a modern urban community in the Delta, offering housing, utilities, public services and recreational spaces.
Other new cities include New October, Hadayek October, East Port Said, New Ismailia, Nasser City in West Assiut, West Qena and West Aswan.
Egypt has developed 39 new cities over the past few years as part of its urban expansion strategy within Vision 2030.

articles.title: U.S. journalist forcibly deported to Dubai sues Kenya, fights to return to East Africa after immigration row - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: U.S. journalist forcibly deported to Dubai sues Kenya, fights to return to East Africa after immigration row  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- American journalist Margot Kiser Jones was deported from Kenya to Dubai after being labeled a prohibited immigrant over alleged security and public morals concerns.
- She claims the Kenyan authorities did not provide due process, as she was not notified of the decision or given a chance to defend herself.
- Jones highlights the contradiction of being granted a three-year residency permit months after her blacklisting, suggesting administrative errors.
- Government officials argue the deportation was lawful, blaming a system misspelling for failure to flag her prohibited status when the permit was issued.
Known for reporting on the high-profile Shakahola trial involving preacher Paul Mackenzie, Jones was removed from the country in March 2026 after authorities designated her a prohibited immigrant.
She is now urging the court to overturn the government's decision and permit her immediate return to the East African country.
American reporter challenges Kenya over sudden deportation to Dubai
According to court filings reported by Tuko, Kenyan authorities placed Jones on the prohibited immigrant list on October 9, 2025, citing a national security report that claimed her presence threatened public morals and safety.
However, officials did not send her back to her home country, the United States, but instead deported her to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates on March 8, 2026.
Jones contends that state officers conducted the entire process without due process.
She asserts that she was never presented with the intelligence report or given an opportunity to defend herself prior to her expulsion.
In a filed affidavit, Jones explained: "By failing to notify me of the decision, the respondents effectively denied me my constitutional right to challenge the decision before its implementation".
Furthermore, she argued that being dropped in Dubai left her stranded without accommodation or contacts, placing her in a precarious situation.
She also pointed out that immigration officials allowed her to travel freely within Kenya for nearly six months after declaring her a threat, casting doubt on the urgency of the security claims.
Contradictory visa records fuel U.S. journalist's fight to return to Kenya
A major element of the legal petition involves a three-year Class K residency permit issued to Jones on February 5, 2026, four months after she was supposedly declared an illegal alien.
Jones argues that receiving official residency approval either invalidates the original ban or gave her a legitimate reason to believe her stay in Kenya was lawful.
In response, government representatives explained that a system misspelling of her surname prevented the database from flagging her prohibited status, though Jones maintains that administrative mistakes remain the state's responsibility.
Government bodies including the Directorate of Immigration Services, the Ministry of Interior, and the Attorney-General defend the action as lawful under the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act, insisting that prohibited individuals cannot reside in the country regardless of permit errors.

articles.title: DARYL SWANEPOEL | Defend Agoa, but let’s resist alarmism - Business Day
articles.summary: DARYL SWANEPOEL | Defend Agoa, but let’s resist alarmism  Business Day
articles.full_text:
South Africa should do everything reasonably within its power to retain the benefits of the African Growth & Opportunity Act (Agoa) and repair its strained relationship with the US. Our economy needs stronger growth, investment and employment. We should expand trade with America while growing our other markets.
However, with an Agoa eligibility announcement expected within the next few weeks we must also consider what happens if diplomacy fails. Preparing for that possibility is responsible economic management. It requires neither indifference towards Agoa nor an invitation to Washington to withdraw it. It requires an honest assessment of the consequences.
That assessment is becoming obscured by alarmist rhetoric. Of late a number of organisations have portrayed the situation as an emergency, citing up to 250,000 jobs partially or fully dependent on Agoa and more than 500,000 associated with US trade. Their policy proposals have reinforced the sense of urgency surrounding the approaching decision.
Concern for those workers is legitimate. But employment associated with trade is not the same as employment that would disappear if a particular preference were withdrawn. The distinction is fundamental. Without it, large employment figures can create an impression of impending national economic disaster without establishing the likelihood or scale of the losses.
We should ask what exclusion would change. Which products would attract additional duties? How much would those duties rise? Which exports would remain competitive? What could be sold elsewhere? These questions matter more than the repeated presentation of the entire trading relationship as though it were about to vanish.
Our preliminary analysis of a South African Revenue Service (Sars) extract places South African merchandise exports to the US in 2025 at about R148bn. Matching identifiable mineral products against the September 2025 reciprocal tariff exemption schedule accounts for about R76bn. Complete motor vehicles account for another R17bn. Deducting these categories leaves some R55bn.
For perspective, that remainder represents about 2.7% of South Africa’s global merchandise exports and 0.73% of nominal GDP in 2025. Sars reported preliminary global merchandise exports of about R2.08-trillion, while Stats SA placed nominal GDP at about R7.6-trillion.
A fuller reconciliation with US import statistics, particularly the classification of additional gold-related imports, could reveal a smaller remaining share of exports after these deductions. The preliminary calculation may therefore overstate that share, though this requires confirmation.
These are measures of scale, not estimates of economic loss. Nor is the remainder a definitive measure of Agoa exposure. Exemption from reciprocal tariffs and exemption from ordinary customs duties under Agoa are different arrangements. Some product classifications require further examination. The calculation nevertheless illustrates why the composition of our exports deserves attention.
Motor vehicles provide a useful example. Covered passenger cars already face an additional 25% automotive tariff. Losing an Agoa preference could add the ordinary passenger-car duty of 2.5%, taking the combined rate to 27.5%. That additional cost matters, but exclusion would not suddenly create the entire new tariff burden confronting the industry. Other vehicle classifications carry different ordinary duties.
Critical minerals must also be considered within America’s strategic interests. Washington explicitly seeks diversified supplies and reduced dependence on adversarial countries, as its January 14 White House fact sheet confirms. Continued access to important South African minerals serves that objective. There are therefore sound reasons to expect favourable treatment for key mineral products to remain attractive to the US, despite diplomatic tensions.
This is an expectation, not an assurance. American policy also seeks to strengthen domestic production and leaves room for tariffs and minimum import prices. South Africa should negotiate actively around these shared supply interests, rather than assume either permanent protection or inevitable exclusion.
Even where additional duties arise, exports do not automatically cease. Buyers may continue purchasing South African products. Costs may be shared through lower exporter margins, importer adjustments and higher consumer prices. Some businesses will find alternative customers. Others will struggle. The outcome depends on competitiveness and commercial responses, rather than simply equalising the value of the exports concerned.
Agoa is a unilateral preference requiring renewal and continued eligibility. South Africa cannot confidently build its economic future around its indefinite continuation.
Agriculture demonstrates the importance of this distinction. Global agricultural exports increased from about $13.7bn in 2024 to $15.1bn in 2025. Agricultural exports to the US were $504m in 2025, down about 3%. This modest decline occurred despite the additional 30% reciprocal tariff imposed on non-exempt South African products from August 7 2025, including those qualifying for duty-free access under Agoa. However, the annual figures capture only about five months of exposure to that higher tariff.
Calculated from these rounded figures, the increase in agricultural exports to markets outside the US was about $1.42bn ― about 2.7 times the previous year’s entire agricultural exports to America. The department of agriculture reported that growth elsewhere more than offset the US losses.
That does not mean every affected farmer found an equally profitable replacement market or that all the growth resulted from redirecting US orders. It does show that diversification can cushion losses. For producers facing a largely fixed harvest in the short term, access to alternative buyers can preserve sales, though prices and margins may differ.
Our objective should be to grow both American and other markets. Agricultural resilience is evidence of our capacity to adapt, not a reason to relinquish valuable customers.
Independent research corroborates the case for proportion. A November 2023 Brookings study estimated that losing Agoa alone would reduce South Africa’s exports to the US by about 2.7% and the national GDP by about 0.06%. Its model allowed for some trade diversion towards other destinations.
The study predates the additional US automotive tariffs introduced in April 2025. Those tariffs already form part of the trading environment and their effects should be incorporated into forecasts that account for the present tariff regime. The relevant question is therefore the further impact of losing Agoa preferences, without counting the existing automotive tariff shock again.
Brookings’ estimates cannot be applied mechanically to today’s circumstances, but they provide corroborating evidence that the loss of Agoa alone need not produce dramatic, immediate economy-wide consequences. But the study does not capture potential investment and confidence effects.
The longer-term question also deserves attention. Agoa is a unilateral preference requiring renewal and continued eligibility. South Africa cannot confidently build its economic future around its indefinite continuation.
In my discussions with US policymakers and legislators since 2015, possible “graduation” was already a recurring theme. Contemporary reporting confirms that some congressional factions regarded South Africa as sufficiently developed to move towards more reciprocal trading arrangements.
Upper-middle-income status did not legally disqualify us, but our relative development supplied a political argument for graduation. The uncertainty therefore predates today’s diplomatic dispute.
Preserving Agoa and preparing for life beyond it are compatible responsibilities. We should pursue constructive diplomacy, protect existing commercial relationships, develop more durable trade arrangements and assist businesses most exposed to additional duties.
None of this discounts the workers and communities for whom even a modest national loss could be devastating. Targeted support requires identifying those risks accurately. Alarmism offers little help in doing so.
South Africa should defend Agoa because it is valuable. We should also assess possible exclusion with evidence and proportion. A clear understanding of our vulnerabilities and capacity to adapt will strengthen our decisions while we continue working for the outcome we want: a healthier relationship with the US and expanding trade with it.
• Swanepoel is CEO of the Inclusive Society Institute.

articles.full_text:
- South Africa stands out as the only African nation featured among the world’s top food destinations for 2026, earning a remarkable 94.26% in the global poll.
- The country’s rich culinary identity blends indigenous flavors, European influences, and local traditions into a unique and vibrant food scene.
- Cape Malay cuisine and the iconic braai form the heart of South Africa’s culinary culture, while coastal regions deliver fresh seafood and cities like Cape Town host world-class restaurants.
- Wine regions add another dimension, creating unforgettable pairing experiences for food-loving travellers.
South Africa has been named among the world’s best countries for food in 2026, emerging as the only African country to feature on the list and putting its diverse culinary scene in the global spotlight.
The country scored 94.26% in the Time Out's 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards, which asked thousands of readers to rate their favourite destinations. Italy claimed the top spot with a score of 96.92%, recognised for its rich regional food traditions, from Naples’ pizza and Sicily’s cannoli to Milan’s risotto.
South Africa’s inclusion highlights the growing international appeal of its food culture, shaped by indigenous traditions, European influences, and the culinary heritage of communities across the country.
A diverse culinary landscape
South African cuisine draws on several cultural influences, creating a food scene that stretches from traditional home cooking to contemporary restaurants and internationally recognised dining experiences.
Cape Malay cuisine, particularly in Cape Town, is known for its aromatic curries, spices and dishes such as bobotie, a baked minced-meat dish often topped with an egg-based custard. Meanwhile, the country's braai culture remains a central part of social life, bringing people together over grilled meat, boerewors and other local favourites.
Coastal destinations offer fresh seafood, while cities such as Cape Town and Johannesburg have developed restaurant scenes that combine local ingredients with international techniques.
The country's wine-producing regions also add to its culinary appeal, attracting visitors interested in food and wine experiences.
Italy leads the global rankings
Italy secured first place with a score of 96.92%, reflecting the international popularity of its regional specialities and long-established culinary traditions.
Its food culture extends well beyond familiar dishes such as pizza and pasta. Visitors can explore seafood along the coast, risotto in northern Italy, pastries in Sicily and a wide range of regional dishes that vary from one part of the country to another.

articles.summary: NEVA MAKGETLA | South Africa’s coal reliance slows its energy transition  Business Day
articles.full_text:
By any standard, South Africa stands out internationally for its high levels of emissions. In 2024 it ranked 36th out of 203 countries on carbon emissions per person. It came in 27th out of 199 for greenhouse gas emissions per dollar of GDP.
South Africa’s average emissions per person were 1.5 times the world’s average, and three times as high relative to GDP. The pattern is the same if we only look at other upper-middle-income countries.
The country’s high emissions result from a combination of energy-intensive production, especially from the metal refineries, dependence on coal for electricity and reliance on roads rather than rail for long-distance freight outside mining.
In terms of energy per dollar of GDP, South Africa uses more than twice the international average. Again, the picture is similar if we only look at peer economies. Its energy intensity arose largely from the push in the 1990s to use cheap, coal-fuelled electricity to attract ferro-alloy and aluminium metal refineries.
Over the past decade these industries downsized sharply as the cost of grid electricity tripled. Still, in 2025 they bought almost a quarter of all electricity from the national grid. But they contributed only about 1% of GDP, 0.4% of formal employment and 2% of exports.
Most countries that promote energy-intensive metal refineries, where electricity is the most expensive input, rely on relatively low-cost (and clean) hydroelectricity, or sometimes nuclear power. In contrast, South Africa mostly promoted coal.
In 2025 coal fuelled 80% of South Africa’s electricity use, compared with about 55% in China and just over 40% in other upper-middle-income countries. Renewables provided under 15% of electricity in South Africa compared with more than 35% in China and 18% in other upper-middle-income countries.
The reliance on coal means South Africa’s emissions intensity dropped over the past decade as electricity use fell about 25%. In 2014 the country emitted 1,600 tonnes of greenhouse gases per $1m GDP; today, the figure is about 1,400 tonnes. The fall mostly resulted from Eskom’s soaring tariffs, which led to the near collapse of the energy-intensive ferro-alloy refineries as well as declining use of grid electricity across the economy.
At the same time, private generation of renewable energy both on and off the grid increased from about 10% of total electricity in the late 2010s to about 20% today.
A second factor in South Africa’s high emissions is the reliance on diesel to ship most goods to and from Gauteng, with rail lines designed primarily for bulk mining exports. Liquid fuels accounted for more than 15% of South Africa’s total imports in 2025, compared with under 10% for peer economies.
South Africa’s uniquely emissions-intensive economy means the shift to cleaner electricity and logistics is immensely disruptive. That has resulted in bitter opposition from companies that built their fortunes on coal and petrol. Eskom in particular seems intent on keeping its older coal plants, built in the 1980s, open beyond their planned obsolescence in the early 2030s.
South Africa’s uniquely emissions-intensive economy means the shift to cleaner electricity and logistics is immensely disruptive. That has resulted in bitter opposition from companies that built their fortunes on coal and petrol.
However, it is risky to ignore technology trajectories, which are defined as successful when their costs drop below existing production techniques while their quality outpaces existing offerings. This is clearly true for renewable energy, and probably also for electric vehicles.
In the latest round of procurement for renewable energy for the grid the cost per kilowatt-hour was about a quarter of Eskom’s latest tariffs. Sales of hybrid and electric cars in South Africa rose from virtually none in the late 2010s to about 5% of sales in 2026, mostly thanks to Chinese imports that compete on both price and quality.
Once customers start voting with their feet, measures to slow the adoption of new technologies risk undermining national competitiveness. We need to find ways to manage the disruption to historic core industries, rather than trying to protect emissions-intensive producers at the cost of future growth in jobs, production and exports.

With VEFTA, Vietnam and Switzerland have more opportunities to cooperate in processing and manufacturing industries, green energy, innovation, human resource development, and leveraging the complementary strengths of the two economies.
On the afternoon of October 18th, in Hanoi, immediately following the signing ceremony of the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA), the Switzerland -Vietnam Economic Forum Hanoi 2026 took place with the participation of the President of the Swiss Confederation and Minister of Economy, Education and Research, Guy Parmelin, along with numerous businesses from both countries.
Speaking at the Forum, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung emphasized: The signing of the Agreement is an important milestone in the economic and trade relations between Vietnam and the EFTA countries.
The agreement was signed after 14 years of negotiations and 21 working sessions, a testament to the political will and persistent efforts of all parties.
The Minister expressed his sincere gratitude to President Guy Parmelin and the negotiating teams for their positive contributions to this outcome.
According to the Minister, the meeting between businesses from both sides immediately after the signing ceremony sent a very clear message: The value of the Agreement must be affirmed by cooperation opportunities that translate into concrete business results.
According to the Minister, the Vietnam-EFTA Agreement opens up new avenues for cooperation in trade in goods, services, investment, and sustainable development.
Tariff preferences will facilitate the expansion of Vietnamese goods' markets and enhance their competitiveness; at the same time, they will help EFTA businesses more effectively exploit the potential of the Vietnamese market.
Rules of origin also facilitate production linkages and supply chain connections between Europe and Southeast Asia.
"In the context of a global economy still fraught with uncertainty, the Agreement establishes a transparent, stable, and predictable cooperation framework that helps businesses feel secure in making long-term investments," the Minister emphasized.

Minister Le Manh Hung stated that Vietnam has a dynamic market, increasingly improved production capacity, and an expanding integration network. Meanwhile, Switzerland and the EFTA countries possess strengths in technology, innovation, finance, and quality. Leveraging the complementary strengths of both sides will open up opportunities to form more efficient and sustainable value chains.
Affirming that Vietnam is entering a new phase of development, aiming for rapid, sustainable growth and enhanced economic self-reliance, Minister Le Manh Hung proposed that businesses from both sides focus on promoting four key areas of cooperation.
Specifically, the focus is on developing the processing and manufacturing industries and supply chains. Vietnam aims to attract investment in precision mechanics, automation, supporting industries, and advanced manufacturing technologies; while simultaneously enhancing the capacity of domestic suppliers and gradually participating more deeply in global value chains.
At the same time, it is necessary to promote energy transition and green growth. Both sides need to expand cooperation on smart grids, energy efficiency, green technologies, eco-industrial parks, and the circular economy.
Furthermore, it is essential to promote innovation, the digital economy, healthcare , and life sciences. Cooperation should focus on technology transfer, enhancing research and development capabilities, and effectively leveraging each party's strengths.
In particular, with regard to human resource development, Vietnam wishes to strengthen cooperation in vocational training, skills development, and improving the quality of the workforce, especially through research and application of Switzerland's dual vocational training experience, linking training with the actual needs of businesses.
The Minister affirmed that the Vietnamese Ministry of Industry and Trade is ready to cooperate with agencies, organizations, and business communities from both sides to concretize these orientations into practical cooperation programs and investment projects.
At the Forum, Minister Le Manh Hung delivered three messages to the business communities of both sides.
For Swiss and EFTA businesses, Vietnam is not only a consumer market, but also a long-term investment destination, a competitive manufacturing region, and a partner in the regional supply network.
