For Vietnamese businesses, the Agreement should be seen as a driving force for technological innovation, improving management capabilities, meeting international standards, building brands, and increasing product value.
On behalf of the Vietnamese Government , the Minister pledged to continue institutional reforms, improve the investment and business environment, effectively implement international commitments, and support businesses in taking advantage of opportunities from the Agreement.
"I believe that the success of the Vietnam-EVFTA Agreement is not measured by the number of tariff lines reduced, but by the projects implemented, technologies transferred, supply chains formed, and competitiveness enhanced," Minister Le Manh Hung expressed, and he believes that, with the determination of the Government and the proactive efforts of the business community, economic and trade relations between Vietnam and Switzerland and other EFTA countries will increasingly develop in a substantive, effective, and sustainable manner.
On the morning of October 18th, in Hanoi, in the presence of General Secretary and President To Lam, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung and representatives from four member countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) officially signed the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA).
Representatives from the EFTA countries participating in the signing included the President of the Swiss Confederation, Minister of Economy, Education and Research Guy Parmelin; the Prime Minister and Minister for Government and Finance of Liechtenstein Brigitte Haas; the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Iceland Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir; and the State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Norway Astrid Bergmål.

articles.title: Power, Scanner Failures Stall Trade At Nigeria’s Borders – NCS - The Whistler Newspaper
articles.summary: Power, Scanner Failures Stall Trade At Nigeria’s Borders – NCS  The Whistler Newspaper
articles.full_text:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and its counterparts in Benin Republic and Cameroon have identified unreliable electricity, non-functional cargo scanners, traffic congestion and poor digital connectivity as major obstacles to efficient cross-border trade.
The three countries are intensifying discussions with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) on a proposed regional border-modernisation programme aimed at addressing the infrastructure and operational challenges.
The initiative targets the Mfum-Ekok border corridor between Nigeria and Cameroon and the Sèmè-Kraké corridor linking Nigeria and Benin, with plans to improve customs procedures, digital infrastructure, cargo monitoring and coordination among border agencies.
However, the NCS said no final project cost, lending commitment, financing arrangement or implementation contract had been agreed upon.
According to a statement issued on Sunday by Abdullahi Maiwada, Deputy Comptroller of Customs and National Public Relations Officer, on behalf of the Comptroller-General of Customs, the discussions took place at Afreximbank’s headquarters in Cairo, Egypt, on October 2, 2026.
The meeting followed a benchmarking mission to the Beitbridge Border Post in Zimbabwe and technical assessments of the two priority border corridors in West and Central Africa.
The engagement was led by Comptroller-General of Customs Bashir Adewale Adeniyi and brought together representatives of the customs administrations of Nigeria, Benin and Cameroon, alongside Afreximbank and technical partners.
According to the NCS, the assessments revealed significant infrastructure and operational shortcomings that could undermine efforts to facilitate legitimate trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The statement reads in part: “A major component of the engagement was the Customs Declaration Exchange System (CDES) designed to facilitate a secure information exchange among Nigeria’s B’ Odogwu platform, Benin’s Webb and Cameroon CAMCIS.
“Built around a common data model, the system is intended to enable export information originating in one country to support the advance preparation of import-manifest information in the receiving country, thereby reducing duplication and improving the predictability of cross-border transactions.
“The receiving Customs administration will remain responsible for validating the information, applying national requirements, conducting risk assessments, and authorising clearance. Although development and technical testing have been undertaken, further country-specific configuration, application programming interface integration, security assurance and pilot acceptance remain necessary before deployment.
“The discussions drew extensively on findings from the July 2026 Beitbridge benchmarking mission and subsequent assessments of the two priority corridors. The Beitbridge experience demonstrated the importance of treating a modern border as an integrated operational ecosystem encompassing traffic segmentation, pre-arrival processing, risk-based controls, cargo scanning, transit monitoring, electronic payments, information technology command centres, utilities, maintenance and effective governance.
“At Mfum- Ekok, the assessment identified gaps in dependable power supply, connectivity, information technology equipment, cybersecurity, technical support, scanner commissioning and coordinated single-stop processing,” it stated.
The NCS explained that the Sèmè-Kraké corridor faces similar challenges, including non-functional cargo-scanning and weighing facilities, traffic congestion, inconsistent operating hours, incomplete joint customs procedures and unresolved responsibilities for maintaining shared infrastructure.
The statement further reads: “At Sèmè-Kraké, key challenges included incomplete joint procedures and live data exchange, nonfunctional cargo-scanning and weighing facilities, unreliable electricity, traffic congestion, inconsistent operating hours and unresolved responsibilities for maintaining shared infrastructure.
“These findings underscore the need to address immediate operational deficiencies alongside a properly assessed and costed long-term modernisation programme.
“To advance the initiative, Afreximbank outlined a proposed two-stage approach beginning with independent engineering assessments and investment-cost studies at the two border posts, followed by the development of separate bankable project packages for the Nigeria± Benin and Nigeria± Cameroon corridors.
“The proposed project-preparation process would cover transaction advisory services, legal due diligence, financial modelling and the identification of appropriate implementation and financing arrangements. The Bank also outlined the potential use of its Project Preparation Facility, while technical partners, TMP and Bergmans Security Consultants and Supplies Limited, expressed willingness in principle to consider self-financing the preparatory work.
“Although no final project cost, lending commitment, borrower designation, financing arrangement or implementation contract was established, participants agreed on the importance of direct site inspections, designated technical focal points, a clear one-, three- and six-month implementation roadmap and a dated action matrix to guide subsequent engagement.
“The Nigeria Customs Service, under the leadership of CGC Bashir Adewale Adeniyi MFR and his management team, reaffirms the commitment to strengthening regional cooperation, modernising border operations and facilitating legitimate trade in line with the objectives of AfCFTA.
“The Service will continue to engage with its counterparts in Benin and Cameroon, Afreximbank and relevant technical partners to advance the required assessments, clarify projectpreparation arrangements and develop practical, sustainable solutions for the two border corridors to promote more efficient cross-border procedures, improve cargo visibility, strengthen coordinated border management and support the development of an integrated African trading environment, the statement added.”

articles.title: What South Africa’s shrinking GDP really means for households and the economy - Cape Argus
articles.summary: What South Africa’s shrinking GDP really means for households and the economy  Cape Argus
articles.full_text:
South Africa’s economy went backwards in the second quarter, but the 0.2% contraction does not tell the full story of what is happening in households.
Just before the latest gross domestic product (GDP) figures were released, IOL’s Economic Health Index took a broader look at 10 measures of the economy, giving the greatest weight to growth and jobs.
The result was a mixed picture. Trade, the rand and electricity supply were among the stronger indicators, while weak growth, unemployment and subdued business confidence weighed heavily on the index.
GDP has now filled in an important part of that picture – and, in some respects, made the contradictions even more apparent. The economy contracted by 0.2% in the second quarter, its first decline since the third quarter of 2024, as mining, manufacturing and trade went backwards.
But there's money
Yet household spending increased 0.4%, contributing 0.3 percentage points to growth and cushioning what would otherwise have been a considerably larger contraction.
PSG senior economist Johann Els said the headline GDP number also needs to be viewed alongside gross domestic expenditure, which measures spending within the economy.
Net exports subtracted 1.1 percentage points from GDP as imports surged 4.9%, compared with a 0.9% increase in exports.
Els said domestic expenditure had been more stable, questioning the significance attached to whether another negative quarter would put South Africa into a technical recession. “Recession or no recession; doesn't matter. I mean, that's, that's not really a question,” he said.
The latest current account figures reinforce the extent of the external hit.
South Africa moved from a R181.6 billion current account surplus in the first quarter to a R205.5bn deficit in the second, as the value of imports jumped by R376.6bn, largely on the back of higher fuel prices.
Consumers are still spending
For South Africans, the GDP figures show consumers remained surprisingly resilient despite the economic contraction. Household spending rose 0.4%, with food and non-alcoholic beverages among the strongest categories.
This broadly backs up what IOL’s pre-GDP index found.
Real retail sales were still growing, and fast-moving consumer goods sales volumes increased in the first half of the year, even as consumer confidence plunged to minus 19.
Investec economist Lara Hodes said the confidence figures showed households were reluctant to make major purchases, while spending on semi-durable goods had declined.
No coffee today
The restaurant trade offers another indication of caution. Stats SA figures show real food and beverage income fell 0.7% in the second quarter compared with a year earlier, while restaurants and coffee shops declined 1.9%.
Property provides a more positive indicator for those who already own homes.
Statistics South Africa data shows that residential property prices increased 7.9% nationally in April from a year earlier, although the gains were uneven, ranging from 11.2% in the Western Cape to 4.8% in Gauteng.
More recent BetterBond data suggest the momentum continued, with home loan applications 11.3% higher than in late 2023 and approval rates rising to 64.5% by the end of August. BetterBond also found homebuying had become more affordable for most age groups as the ratio between house prices and incomes declined.
But jobs remain the problem
The biggest weakness identified by IOL’s index before the GDP release remains employment.
South Africa’s unemployment rate rose to 33.6% in the second quarter, from 32.7%, as the number of unemployed people increased by 345,000 to 8.5 million. Employment declined by 16,000 to 16.74 million.
The Altron FinTech Household Financial Resilience Index provides another view of what employment losses mean at household level.
It found household finances were stronger than a year earlier, helped by lower interest rates, but weakened during the first quarter as employment, private-sector salaries and household spending came under pressure.
Formal-sector employment fell by 190,000 during the quarter, while life insurance policy surrenders increased 24.3% from a year earlier.
The big issue
Altron FinTech MD Johan Gellatly said employment was driving the deterioration. “Households are not spending their way into difficulty; they are running out of earners,” he said.
The GDP figures do not yet show a collapse in household spending, but the sectors behind the contraction are also significant employers.
Mining contracted 3% during the second quarter, manufacturing fell 1.8% and trade declined 1.9%. The latest figures show mining weakness has since deepened, with production falling 7.5% year-on-year in July, led by platinum group metals, coal and iron ore.
Manufacturing offered some relief, with production increasing 1.1%, although Hodes noted that the improvement was not broad-based and confidence among manufacturers remained subdued.
Investment still missing
The other warning sign is investment.
Gross fixed capital formation – spending on assets such as machinery, equipment and infrastructure that expand future productive capacity – declined 0.2% in the second quarter, its second consecutive quarterly fall. Private businesses and public corporations both reduced investment.
That weakness has not escaped government.
The third phase of the Government-Business Partnership launched this week is explicitly aimed at moving from stabilising electricity, logistics and other constraints towards investment, economic activity and employment.
Its immediate target is growth above 3%, with a focus on labour-intensive growth and expanding industrial capacity. For now, however, the post-GDP picture looks remarkably similar to the one IOL’s index produced before the figures landed.
Consumers are still spending, property prices are rising and improvements in electricity supply remain intact. But the economy has contracted, investment remains weak and unemployment has risen.
The latest numbers therefore leave the central weakness identified by IOL’s Economic Health Index relatively unchanged: South Africa is still struggling to turn its stronger economic indicators into sustained growth and jobs.

articles.summary: South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at $489.1 billion in latest rankings, but sluggish growth and high unemployment cloud its dominance  CediRates
articles.full_text:
General
South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at $489.1 billion in latest rankings, but sluggish growth and high unemployment cloud its dominance
South Africa has retained its position as Africa’s largest economy in the International Monetary Fund’s latest rankings, with a projected gross domestic product of $489.08 billion in 2026, despite persistent unemployment, sluggish growth and weak investment.
Business Insider Africa
published: Oct 18, 2026
South Africa has retained its position as Africa’s largest economy in the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest rankings, with a projected gross domestic product (GDP) of $489.08 billion in 2026, despite persistent unemployment, sluggish growth and weak investment.
- South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy according to IMF projections for 2026, with a GDP of $489.08 billion.
- Despite its economic size, the country faces slow growth, weak investment, and persistent infrastructure challenges.
- Public debt is projected to reach 78.5% of GDP, further limiting fiscal flexibility and growth prospects.
- Government reforms target electricity and logistics, but greater investment, job creation, and infrastructure upgrades are needed for sustained competitiveness.
Figures from the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook place South Africa ahead of Egypt, Nigeria and Algeria, reaffirming its position as the continent’s largest economy by nominal GDP.
Egypt ranks second with $442.89 billion, followed by Nigeria at $386.67 billion and Algeria at $331.89 billion. Morocco completes the top five with $195.63 billion.
South Africa’s economy is $46.19 billion larger than Egypt’s and $102.41 billion ahead of Nigeria’s.
The country's position reflects its established financial services, mining, manufacturing and retail sectors.
However, its economic strength has not translated into faster growth or sufficient employment opportunities.
Slow growth weighs on economic performance
South Africa continues to record modest growth compared with several other major African economies, constrained by weak domestic demand, infrastructure challenges and subdued private investment.
The IMF projected economic growth of 1.4% in 2026, below the rates expected in Ethiopia, Uganda and Tanzania.
Statistics South Africa reported that the economy contracted by 0.2% in the second quarter of 2026, reversing the 0.4% growth recorded in the preceding quarter.
Mining, manufacturing and trade contributed to the decline, while freight rail inefficiencies, port congestion and infrastructure constraints continued to affect businesses.
Unemployment remains stubbornly high
South Africa's unemployment rate increased to 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, up from 32.7% in the previous quarter, according to Statistics South Africa.
The number of unemployed people rose by 345,000 to 8.5 million, while employment declined by 16,000 to 16.7 million.
Youth unemployment remains particularly severe, reflecting limited job opportunities, skills mismatches and weak economic growth.
The labour market challenges have continued to weigh on household incomes and consumer spending, reinforcing concerns about the country's ability to convert economic output into broader prosperity.
Investment and debt pressures persist
South Africa also faces challenges attracting sufficient investment to support faster economic expansion.
An October 2026 Financial Times report indicated that only about half of the R1.5 trillion in investment pledges secured since 2018 had materialised, while fixed investment had declined in four of the previous six quarters.
Public debt remains another concern. The IMF's February 2026 assessment projected government debt at 78.5% of GDP in 2026, limiting fiscal flexibility.
President Cyril Ramaphosa's administration has pursued electricity and logistics reforms to improve business conditions and encourage private sector investment.
Despite these efforts, South Africa continues to face pressure to accelerate growth and employment creation as other African economies expand more rapidly.
While its financial system and industrial base continue to underpin its economic leadership, sustained investment, infrastructure improvements and job creation remain essential to maintaining its competitiveness.

articles.title: World Bank targets fivefold increase in critical-minerals business towards sustainable development - Ghana News Agency
articles.summary: World Bank targets fivefold increase in critical-minerals business towards sustainable development  Ghana News Agency
articles.full_text:
By Francis Ntow, GNA Special Correspondent, Bangkok  
Bangkok, Oct. 17, GNA – The World Bank is targeting a fivefold increase in its critical-minerals business, with a new initiative to help resource-rich countries develop local industries, create jobs and retain more economic value from their mineral resources.  
World Bank President Ajay Banga announced the initiative on the sidelines of the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Group (WBG) annual meetings in Bangkok.  
It will be implemented over the next five years.   
“In critical minerals, we plan to quintuple our business in five years. This week, we launched our first country compacts with Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) partners – to build local industries and keep more jobs and value at home,” Mr Banga stated.  
The Bank has identified 20 countries with which it can partner to advance the initiative.  
Eight countries – Argentina, Bolivia, Egypt, India, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mauritania and Zambia – have already launched their priorities, commitments and measurable targets under the compacts.  
The plans outline reforms to modernise mineral licensing and geological data systems, strengthen environmental oversight, expand infrastructure and develop local skills to attract investment and deliver lasting benefits to communities.  
With Africa holding significant reserves of minerals essential to the energy transition and the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), including cobalt, copper, lithium and manganese, the initiative offers opportunities to develop domestic processing and manufacturing industries.  
Mr Banga said the Bank would work with the identified countries to translate their mineral wealth into tangible development outcomes.  
“Different sectors. Different countries. Different solutions. Same objective: advance development and generate jobs. The next phase is execution at scale,” he said.  
The critical minerals initiative forms part of a broader World Bank jobs agenda, against projections that about 1.2 billion young people would enter the labour market over the next 10 to 15 years, while only about 400 million jobs would be created, leaving a potential shortfall of 800 million.  
Mr Banga said building industries around mineral resources could help narrow the gap by enabling producing countries to move beyond extraction into processing, manufacturing and related services.  
He cited infrastructure development as another key driver of investment and job creation, saying the World Bank, in partnership with the European Commission’s Global Gateway and the United States International Development Finance Corporation, launched 52 new corridor projects last year.  
This had come up from 20 three years earlier.  
The projects seek to link infrastructure with investment and economic opportunities across participating countries.  
“The infrastructure connects places. The opportunity grows along the way,” he said.  
Mr Banga cited the Lobito Corridor in Central Africa as an example, saying the route, initially developed primarily to transport minerals, was increasingly helping farmers move their produce to markets and supporting the growth of towns and cities along the corridor.  
On private capital mobilisation, he said the World Bank had increased the amount mobilised from about US$35 billion in 2022 to US$112 billion, while its total financing had risen to US$230 billion.  
Nearly 55 per cent of the financing had gone into infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health, tourism and value-added manufacturing.  
These sectors are considered important for raising productivity and creating jobs.  
Mr Banga acknowledged that mobilising commercial capital remained particularly difficult in low-income countries, where the amount stood at US$3 billion.  
Nonetheless,  mobilisation had increased fourfold in upper-middle-income countries.  
He said the next phase would focus on expanding operations and investment opportunities, including strengthening the Bank’s presence in New York, Frankfurt, Milan and Tokyo to develop project pipelines and engage investors.  
“That means meeting private-sector clients where they invest and make decisions. But stronger pipelines are only part of the answer,” he said.  
Mr Banga said six multilateral development banks were also developing common approaches to assess, document, package and transfer investments, thus enabling projects initially financed by development institutions to attract other long-term investors.  
“Pension funds, insurers, and sovereign wealth funds manage enormous pools of long-term capital looking for long-term investments. We are making the introduction,” he said.  
Reflecting on the global challenges that prompted the establishment of the World Bank in 1944, Mr Banga said the world faced a new set of challenges that required collective action to expand economic opportunities.  
“The jobs gap is a projection. It does not have to be our future. We have begun to show what this model can deliver. Now we must give it the scale and pace the next generation demands. That future is ours to build. Let us build,” he said.

articles.title: Customs, Afreximbank plan modern border facilities to boost African trade - The Sun Nigeria
articles.summary: Customs, Afreximbank plan modern border facilities to boost African trade  The Sun Nigeria
articles.full_text:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) have deepened talks on plans to modernise Nigeria’s borders with Benin and Cameroon to make the movement of goods across African countries faster and easier.
The proposed programme is aimed at reducing delays at border posts, improving the exchange of trade information and strengthening regional trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The discussions involved the Customs administrations of Nigeria, Benin and Cameroon and were held at Afreximbank’s headquarters in Cairo, Egypt, on October 12, 2026.
The meeting, led by the Comptroller General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, followed a study visit to the Beitbridge Border Post in Zimbabwe and technical assessments of the Mfum–Ekok and Sèmè–Kraké border corridors linking Nigeria with Cameroon and Benin, respectively. The participants examined ways to combine modern technology with better infrastructure and coordinated procedures to improve border operations.
The proposed improvements include digital systems for sharing Customs information, cargo scanners, weighing facilities, access roads, reliable electricity, better internet connectivity and improved traffic management.
The discussions also covered the development of common procedures for handling goods, training for Customs personnel and arrangements to guarantee the movement of goods across national borders.
A key part of the plan is the Customs Declaration Exchange System (CDES), which is designed to allow the three countries to exchange trade information securely.
The system will connect Nigeria’s B’Odogwu platform with Benin’s Customs Webb and Cameroon’s CAMCIS, allowing information provided to Customs in an exporting country to be used in preparing import documents in the receiving country.
This is expected to reduce repeated paperwork, improve the flow of information and help businesses and transport operators plan cross-border shipments more reliably.
However, Customs authorities in the receiving country will retain the power to verify the information, apply their national rules, assess risks and approve the release of goods.
Although the system has undergone development and technical testing, further adjustments, security checks and pilot trials are required before it can be deployed.
The assessments of the two border corridors identified several challenges that must be addressed to achieve the programme’s objectives.
At the Mfum–Ekok border between Nigeria and Cameroon, the team identified unreliable electricity and internet services, inadequate information technology equipment, cybersecurity concerns and delays in commissioning cargo scanners. The need for stronger coordination between the two countries was also highlighted.
At the Sèmè–Kraké border between Nigeria and Benin, the challenges included traffic congestion, unreliable power supply, incomplete joint operating procedures, poor exchange of live data and non-functional cargo-scanning and weighing facilities.
Differences in operating hours and uncertainty over responsibility for maintaining shared infrastructure were also identified as issues requiring attention.
The experience at the Beitbridge Border Post showed the importance of treating a modern border as a coordinated system rather than simply providing new buildings and equipment. Effective operations also require advance processing of cargo information, electronic payments, traffic control, cargo monitoring, reliable utilities and clear management responsibilities.
To move the programme forward, Afreximbank proposed a two-stage approach, beginning with independent engineering assessments and estimates of the investment required at the two border posts.
The next stage would involve preparing separate investment proposals for the Nigeria–Benin and Nigeria–Cameroon corridors. These would include financial assessments, legal reviews, advisory services and plans for implementing and financing the projects.
Afreximbank also indicated that its Project Preparation Facility could support the preparatory work, while technical partners expressed willingness in principle to consider funding the initial studies themselves.
However, the meeting did not produce a final project cost, confirmed loan commitment, financing agreement or implementation contract.
Participants instead agreed on the need for direct inspections of the border facilities, the appointment of technical representatives and a timetable setting out actions to be taken within one, three and six months.
The Nigeria Customs Service said it would continue working with its counterparts in Benin and Cameroon, Afreximbank and other partners to complete the assessments and develop practical plans for modernising the two corridors.
The initiative is expected to support the AfCFTA, which seeks to increase trade among African countries by making it easier for businesses to move goods across borders and access markets across the continent.

articles.summary: Nigeria, Benin, Cameroon Partner Afreximbank to Modernise Borders, Ease Cross-Border Trade for Businesses  MSME Africa
articles.full_text:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and the customs administrations of Benin and Cameroon are working with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) on a regional border modernisation programme aimed at easing cross-border trade, improving cargo movement and supporting implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The initiative targets infrastructure gaps, inefficient customs procedures and limited digital information exchange along the Nigeria-Benin and Nigeria-Cameroon corridors. If implemented, the proposed measures could help businesses involved in regional trade navigate customs processes and move goods more efficiently.
According to a statement issued in Abuja on Sunday by NCS spokesperson Abdullahi Maiwada, discussions on the programme took place at Afreximbank’s headquarters in Cairo, Egypt, on October 12, 2026.
The meeting, led by Comptroller-General of Customs Bashir Adeniyi, brought together representatives of the three countries’ customs administrations, Afreximbank and technical partners to review corridor assessment findings and identify priority interventions.
A key area of discussion was the proposed Customs Declarations Exchange System (CDES), which would enable secure information exchange between the digital customs platforms of Nigeria, Benin and Cameroon.
The system is designed to connect Nigeria’s B’Odogwu platform, Benin’s Customs Webb and Cameroon’s Customs Information System (CAMCIS). It would allow export information generated in one country to support advance preparation of import documentation in the receiving country.
Maiwada said the proposed system uses a common data model to improve information sharing and facilitate faster cross-border processing. However, the receiving country’s customs administration would retain responsibility for validating information, applying national regulations, conducting risk assessments and authorising cargo clearance.
Although development and technical testing have been undertaken, further country-specific configuration, application programming interface integration, security assessments and pilot acceptance are required before the system can be deployed.
The discussions also covered Afreximbank’s potential participation in the next Customs Partnership for African Cooperation in Trade (C-PACT) and progress towards regional and continental transit guarantee arrangements. These measures are intended to strengthen coordination among customs authorities, improve cargo visibility and reduce procedural bottlenecks affecting regional trade.
Assessments of the two priority corridors identified infrastructure and operational challenges that could affect the success of the modernisation programme.
At the Mfum-Ekok border between Nigeria and Cameroon, the assessment highlighted unreliable electricity, poor connectivity, inadequate information technology equipment, cybersecurity concerns and insufficient technical support. It also identified the need to commission cargo scanners and coordinate single-stop border processing.
At the Sèmè-Kraké corridor linking Nigeria and Benin, the assessment found gaps in joint operating procedures and real-time data exchange, alongside non-functional cargo scanning and weighing facilities.
The corridor also faces unreliable electricity, traffic congestion, inconsistent operating hours and unresolved responsibilities for maintaining shared infrastructure.
Maiwada said the findings reinforced the need to address immediate operational shortcomings while developing a long-term modernisation programme supported by proper assessments and cost estimates.
A benchmarking mission to Zimbabwe’s Beitbridge Border Post in July 2026 also informed the discussions. Participants examined approaches to infrastructure development, traffic management, pre-arrival processing and risk-based controls that could be incorporated into an efficient border management system.
To advance the initiative, Afreximbank proposed a two-stage project preparation process, beginning with independent engineering assessments and investment-cost studies at the Mfum-Ekok and Sèmè-Kraké border posts.
The second stage would involve developing separate bankable project packages for the Nigeria-Cameroon and Nigeria-Benin corridors.
According to the NCS, the proposed preparation process would cover transaction advisory services, legal due diligence, financial modelling and the identification of appropriate financing and implementation arrangements. Afreximbank also outlined the potential use of its Project Preparation Facility to support the work.
Technical partners TMP and Bergmans Security Consultants and Supplies Limited expressed willingness in principle to consider self-financing the preparatory work.
However, the meeting did not establish a final project cost, lending commitment, designated borrower, financing structure or implementation contract.
The border modernisation discussions come amid wider efforts to improve trade under the AfCFTA framework. Earlier in 2026, the AfCFTA Secretariat selected Nigeria as a pilot country for implementing its Simplified Trade Regime (STR) in West Africa, according to Nairametrics.
The framework is designed to simplify cross-border trade procedures for small-scale traders, potentially making it easier for them to access regional markets and participate in intra-African commerce.
An AfCFTA Secretariat delegation led by Pedro Estevao subsequently engaged with the Nigeria Customs Service at its headquarters in Abuja to advance implementation of the regime.
For businesses trading between Nigeria and neighbouring countries, the proposed border reforms could create opportunities for more predictable customs procedures and improved cargo movement. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on infrastructure upgrades, successful digital integration and the implementation of the proposed measures.

articles.title: Cyril Ramaphosa tells South Africa to prepare for loss of U.S.-Africa trade deal - The Hindu
articles.summary: Cyril Ramaphosa tells South Africa to prepare for loss of U.S.-Africa trade deal  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Monday (October 19, 2026) the country should “prepare” for the possibility of being removed from Washington’s duty-free trade programme for Africa, as ties between the two nations continue to fray.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the U.S. market, has been renewed until the end of 2028.
South Africa is the scheme’s largest beneficiary but its eligibility has come under scrutiny as Washington steps up criticism of Pretoria, including false allegations of discrimination against white Afrikaners that South Africa rejects.
“Congress has decided that we should be kept in AGOA. What now remains is the executive,” Mr. Ramaphosa said, referring to the pact now needing President Donald Trump’s signature after approval by Congress.
“And by the way, so that I prepare our people for this, if we ever have a choice, we are not the first and only country to be taken out of AGOA. And I believe we will not be the last,” he said in response to a question from an AFP journalist during a briefing.
Bilateral ties have deteriorated since Mr. Trump took office, with Washington cutting aid, expelling South Africa’s ambassador and berating Mr. Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a “white genocide”.
Washington in mid-September announced restrictions on visas for South Africans who promote “race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa” -- all issues that are disputed between the two countries.
Last year, the United States launched a programme to resettle white Afrikaners who say they face persecution and violent crime in South Africa.
By September 30, the United States had admitted 16,287 South Africans under the programme over the preceding year. They were the only people granted refugee status by Washington during that period, apart from five Afghans.
‘Devastating’ impact’
The U..S president reviews countries’ eligibility for AGOA annually.
Any removal requires 60 days’ notice to Congress and the country concerned. To take effect on January 1, an exclusion must be announced by November 2.
Former president Joe Biden declared the Central African Republic, Gabon, Niger and Uganda ineligible on October 30, 2023, with the exclusions taking effect on January 1, 2024.
“South Africa is going to look for alternative markets to minimise the impacts of such an exclusion,” Mr. Ramaphosa said.
“I need as president to prepare us if it ever happens. So we should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world,” he said, conceding that the impacts would nonetheless be “devastating”.
Within AGOA, Washington exempts South African cars from customs duties.
After precious metals, cars are the country’s second-biggest export earner to the United States, according to the South African tax authorities.
In 2025, the automobile employers’ organisation Naamsa said 86,000 jobs were directly tied to the accord at car manufacturers, a number that increases to 125,000 when including their sub-contractors.

Lithium cost pass-through drives volatile quarter for energy storage cells: Cell Price Review Q3 2026
Battery cell prices fell across nearly every grade in Q3 2026, but the path differed sharply by format. For instance, Benchmark’s LFP Prismatic 314Ah EXW China and CIF Europe prices ended the quarter lower after a pronounced July spike, Benchmark’s LFP Prismatic 314Ah CIF North America prices were broadly unchanged, and the Benchmark Lithium Ion Battery Global price closed the quarter at its lowest level of the period. "Overall, Q3 was defined by the delayed transmission of lithium volatility into cell pricing, most visibly in ESS formats, alongside a regional divergence that left North American prices at a premium to Europe by quarter-end as freight costs rose," said Adam Megginson, a principal price analyst at Benchmark.

UK considering alignment with EU over tariff on Chinese EVs
While countries including the US, Turkey, and Mexico have been ramping up tariffs on electric vehicles (EVs) made in China, EV imports from China into the UK have continued to face a standard 10% import duty. The UK’s largest trading partner, the EU, introduced tariffs on China-made BEVs in 2024. In 2023, the last year when EVs made in China did not face additional tariffs from the EU, they accounted for 17% of total EV sales within the bloc. They broadly maintained this share until 2026, when over the first eight months of the year that share increased to 22% as Chinese automakers push into overseas markets against the backdrop of their subdued domestic environment. In comparison, China-made EVs accounted for 19% of EV sales in the UK in 2023, with that figure rising to 33% so far in 2026.
Oct 06, 2026
Can Cobre Panama copper mine run for 25 years without growing?
A commission convened by Panama’s government to decide how to manage the country’s controversial Cobre Panama copper mine has recommended 25 years of operation but without expanding the site’s physical footprint. The mine, run by First Quantum Minerals, was closed in 2023 after it was ruled unconstitutional following protests against its operation. The report also recommends steadily shrinking the existing footprint over this time, before eight years of “active closure” and 30 years of post-closure monitoring. Other non-negotiable criteria for reopening the site include compliance with existing Supreme Court rulings and laws around the project, ownership by the state, and the project must be financially self-sustaining. The report also calls for data transparency and supervision of the site to international standards, and priority given to concerns among affected Panamanian communities and businesses.

Lithium price reversal gets respite then deepens: Q3 2026 Lithium Price Review
Both lithium chemical and feedstock prices fell notably across Q3 2026, extending the lithium price correction that began in Q2. A volatile decline through July gave way to a notable August rally, before a sharp September reversal that erased the quarter's gains in a matter of days.

How can African nations benefit from the region’s battery mineral resources?
In recent years, Africa has rapidly grown from a small player in the global battery supply chain to a strategically significant one, as global players begin to realise the potential of the region’s resources. As Europe and North America in particular look to diversify their China-centric supply chains, African nations are emerging as key trade partners. Africa’s growing role in the global battery supply chain and how countries in the region can best capture value from this were key points of discussion at Benchmark’s Giga Africa event in Marrakesh, Morocco.

Brazil’s EV charging network shifts into the fast lane
Brazil’s electric vehicle (EV) landscape is entering a new era of maturity thanks to growth in its charging network. What started as a handful of pilot projects has turned into a fast-growing, mature network built to meet the rapid growth in Brazil's EV demand. Recent data from Benchmark's EV Charging Service highlights a fundamental shift toward high-power, rapid-charging infrastructure capable of supporting both surging consumer adoption and heavy commercial logistics.

Increased DRC exports led to cobalt hydroxide prices (CIF Asia) falling 31% to across Q3 to $17.25/lb ($38,030/tonne), while cobalt sulphate prices (EXW China) dropped nearly 30% to RMB 58,000/tonne ($8,642), according to Benchmark’s Cobalt Price Assessment. EXW Europe cobalt metal prices eased about 11%, while CIF Asia MHP cobalt payables sank from 91.5% to 65.8% by mid September as a result of cheaper hydroxide offering an alternative. “Q3 2026 has seen a broad decline in prices across the cobalt supply chain as rising DRC-origin supply succeeded the weak downstream buying that defined Q2,” said George Ingall, a senior cobalt price analyst at Benchmark.

Export interventions and payables under pressure: Q3 2026 Black Mass Price Review
Benchmark’s NCM Black Mass EXW China payables have fallen 4.9% since the end of Q2, from 77.0% to 73.3%. articles.title: Zimbabwe moves up Africa’s largest economy rankings at $65.9 billion, but heavy US dollar reliance has not helped it match Tanzania’s growth - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Zimbabwe moves up Africa’s largest economy rankings at $65.9 billion, but heavy US dollar reliance has not helped it match Tanzania’s growth  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Zimbabwe is projected to be Africa’s 14th largest economy in 2026 with a GDP of $65.92 billion, supported by agriculture and mining recovery.
- Zimbabwe’s economic growth is forecast at 5% for 2026, lower than Tanzania’s projected 5.9%, due in part to different monetary policies.
- Zimbabwe continues to face persistent challenges from high inflation, currency volatility, and significant debt arrears, restricting access to international finance.
- Tanzania, in contrast, has strengthened the use of its national currency, seen stronger GDP growth, and diversified through major energy and infrastructure investments.
According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook, Zimbabwe ranks 14th among Africa’s largest economies, ahead of Cameroon at $64.81 billion and Tunisia at $62.74 billion.
The latest position marks an improvement from earlier IMF estimates, which placed the country 17th in 2025 with GDP of $51.22 billion. In April 2026, the Fund ranked it 16th at $56.71 billion, before revising its projections in October.
The southern African economy is expected to grow by 5% in 2026, following an estimated 8.3% expansion in 2025, supported by favourable gold prices, recovering agricultural production and remittance inflows.
Despite these gains, Zimbabwe trails Tanzania, whose economy is projected at $96.18 billion, $30.26 billion larger, with growth forecast at 5.9% in 2026.
The two countries also differ in currency policy, with Zimbabwe heavily reliant on the US dollar while Tanzania has strengthened the use of its national currency in domestic transactions.
Zimbabwe's recovery highlights currency challenges
Years of high inflation, currency depreciation and repeated monetary reforms have weakened confidence in Zimbabwe's local currency, driving widespread use of the US dollar.
In April 2024, the government introduced the Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) to replace its previous currency and restore monetary stability.
Despite the reform, the US dollar remains dominant, accounting for about two-thirds of payments by value in the national payment system, according to the IMF's May 2026 assessment.
The currency transition also affected major businesses, including Econet Wireless Zimbabwe, founded by billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, which adjusted its payment systems to accommodate the ZiG.
While continued reliance on the US dollar has helped households and businesses protect their finances against local currency depreciation, it has limited the central bank's control over monetary policy.
In response, authorities tightened monetary measures to stabilise prices and exchange rates, with annual ZiG inflation reaching 3.7% in September 2026, up from 2.9% in August, according to the Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency.
The IMF acknowledged improvements in economic stability in its August assessment but called for continued fiscal discipline and reforms to strengthen confidence in the financial system.
Despite these gains, Zimbabwe's history of currency instability complicates comparisons of its economic performance with other African countries.
Nominal GDP expressed in US dollars is influenced by exchange rates and national accounting methods, meaning currency movements can change international rankings without corresponding changes in production.
This is particularly relevant to Zimbabwe, whose national accounts were redenominated following the introduction of the ZiG in 2024, according to the IMF's October 2026 database.
Consequently, the country's projected $65.92 billion GDP reflects its economic output in dollar terms rather than providing a direct measure of monetary stability or living standards.
Tanzania offers a different economic picture
Tanzania, meanwhile, has pursued a different approach to currency management, taking steps to strengthen the use of the Tanzanian shilling in domestic transactions.
In March 2025, the government introduced regulations requiring businesses to price goods and services and accept payments in shillings, subject to specified exceptions.
Alongside these measures, agriculture, construction, mining, tourism and infrastructure investment have supported economic growth.
The country is also pursuing a proposed $42 billion liquefied natural gas project involving international energy companies, although a final investment decision remains pending.
Tanzania's faster projected growth reflects these broader economic activities and investment trends rather than currency policy alone. Both countries remain exposed to exchange rate pressures and external economic risks.
